title: Waiting Without Spinning: Condition Variables, the Lost Wakeup, and Stopping a Thread That Is Asleep

questions.question: A consumer needs to wait for a producer. It loops, calling try_pop and yield until an item arrives. What does that cost while nothing happens?
options: Nothing, since yield gives the CPU away
A whole core: measured over 100 ms, a spinning consumer used 100.05 ms of CPU across more than 230,000 polls
About one percent of a core
It depends only on the size of the queue
questions.explanation: yield gives up the time slice and the thread is immediately runnable again, so it finds out that nothing happened as fast as the machine allows. A condition variable waiter used 0.04 ms for the same 100 ms.

questions.question: notify_one is called while no thread is waiting. A thread then calls wait_for(lock, 50 ms) with no condition checked. What happens?
options: It wakes at once, since a notification was sent
It times out: a condition variable does not remember a notification nobody heard
It throws an exception
It waits for ever
questions.explanation: Measured: timed out. The same wait that first asked whether a flag was set returned at once. The thing waited for is state under the mutex, and the notification only says look again.

questions.question: Why is the wait in pop_for a while loop (while items_.empty() && !closed_) and not an if?
options: Loops are faster
A wakeup only says look again: another consumer may have taken the item first, and the standard allows a wait to return with nobody having notified
Because wait_until can only be called in a loop
To make the code shorter
questions.explanation: Measured with two consumers and one item: one took it and the other had to carry on waiting. A spurious wakeup is allowed even when nothing changed, so the condition is always rechecked.

questions.question: Three consumers are asleep in pop_for. close() uses notify_one instead of notify_all. What happens?
options: All three wake, since the queue is closed
One wakes and returns closed; the other two stay asleep until their deadlines, and a program waiting to join them cannot exit
None of them wake
It does not compile
questions.explanation: Every waiter has to notice, so every waiter has to be woken. With notify_all, the measured result was all three returned closed within 1 ms of a 5000 ms wait.

questions.question: The GCC 11 thread sanitizer reports a double lock inside a push, which is only a lock_guard, in a program that waits with wait_until(steady_clock). What is going on?
options: A real deadlock, fixed by using system_clock
A tool limitation: GCC 11's sanitizer does not intercept pthread_cond_clockwait, so it never sees the mutex released during the wait. clang 14's reports nothing
A bug in lock_guard
A data race in the queue
questions.explanation: Measured on a twelve line program: 2 warnings on gcc 11, none on clang 14, and none for wait() or system_clock. Switching to system_clock would silence it and make the timeout jump when the clock is adjusted.

questions.question: Why does every wait in this lesson's queue take a deadline?
options: Because wait_until requires one
A control path that waits for ever on a producer that has died has stopped controlling, and a test that waits for ever on a queue nobody wrote to is a hung test
To make the code slower on purpose
Deadlines let the queue be lock free
questions.explanation: A timeout is a result like any other, kTimeout beside kGot and kClosed. It is also the second line of defence for shutdown: a consumer that wakes at least occasionally can notice a stop request even if a notification is missed.
